title: 808 machine kit
notes:
The drum machine, not a room. All four kits on the shelf are rooms — a neutral one, a western one, a rock one and a jazz one — and every genre whose identity *is* a machine (`trap`, `hiphop`, and the whole synth-pop end) had nothing but a quieter version of a drum kit.

The defining fact of an 808 is that **its kick is a pitched instrument with a one-second decay**, which is a category difference rather than a tuning one. Kick decay 1.2 s against `house-kit`'s 0.4, `pitchDecay` 0.06 against 0.03, and — the important one — **`octaves` down to 2 from 6**. A big sweep is a *thump*: the pitch falls through six octaves in 30 ms and what you hear is a transient. A small sweep over a long decay is a *note*: it lands almost immediately on G0 and then simply holds, which is why an 808 kick carries the bass line and why `bass/moog-sub` has to leave room for it rather than doubling it. Two of them at different pitches make a riff, and that riff will be the loudest thing in the mix.

**The clap is the backbeat, not the snare.** Level 0.72 against the snare's 0.5, inverting `house-kit`'s ordering. A 1 kHz burst at Q 1.6 with a 0.22 s decay — narrower and much longer than the house clap's 0.12 s, because the 808 clap is really several bursts smeared into one and the tail is where that lives. Anything wanting a struck snare on 2 and 4 should be reaching for `slab-kit`; this kit's 2 and 4 is a clap.

**The snare is thin on purpose.** 1.9 kHz, 0.1 s, Q 1.3 — up in frequency and cut in half in time against the house snare's 1.4 kHz / 0.18 s, and its `snareBody` drops to level 0.28 with a 0.06 s decay. A machine snare has almost no shell in it; adding body back is what makes a programmed beat sound like a badly-recorded real one.

**Hats are metallic and tiny.** 9 kHz at 0.025 s closed — higher and shorter than anything else on the shelf — because an 808 hat is a bank of square oscillators through a high-pass, and what survives is a tick. The open hat runs 0.5 s, long enough to be an event rather than a longer tick.

**Toms are pure sine drops**, sharing the kick's DNA: `pitchDecay` 0.08, `octaves` 1.5, decays around 0.7 s. On a real kit a tom is a drum; on an 808 it is the kick voice retuned, and modelling that honestly is what keeps the fills sounding like the same machine.

The rim is a 1.7 kHz spike at 0.02 s — the 808 rimshot, which is a click with a pitch and no body at all. Shaker sits low and pink, as the one piece here that is not synthetic in character.
summary: Drum machine, not a room: a one-second pitched kick that carries the bass line, clap over snare. Trap and hiphop.
